concept.name: Swap
concept.definition: A derivative in which two counterparties agree to exchange streams of cash flows over a specified period, computed by applying agreed rates, prices, or formulas to a notional amount. Under the detailed statutory definition in the Commodity Exchange Act (as amended by the Dodd-Frank Act), the term includes interest rate swaps, commodity swaps, currency swaps, equity swaps, and credit default swaps.
concept.intuition: A swap lets two parties trade one kind of payment obligation for another — for example, exchanging a fixed interest bill for a floating one — without trading the underlying asset itself.
concept.mechanics: Cash flows are typically netted on each payment date against a notional principal that is usually not exchanged. Swaps are documented under ISDA master agreements; post-Dodd-Frank, many standardized swaps must be centrally cleared through a derivatives clearing organization, executed on swap execution facilities, and reported to swap data repositories.
concept.formula: Net payment on a payment date = Notional x (rate paid - rate received) x day-count fraction.
concept.failure_modes: Uncleared swaps carry bilateral counterparty credit risk over long tenors. Hedged exposures can mismatch the swap's terms (basis risk), and benchmark transitions (e.g., LIBOR cessation) can strand legacy contracts.
concept.misconceptions: That the notional principal changes hands — in most swaps it never does and exists only to compute payments. Also, swaps are often seen as exotic speculation, but their most common use is routine balance-sheet hedging.
concept.example: A company with floating-rate debt enters a five-year pay-fixed/receive-floating interest rate swap on $50 million notional, converting its interest expense to a fixed rate.

citations.source: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry
